source.title: Multi-D magnetohydrodynamic modelling of pulsar wind nebulae: recent progress and open questions

accepted.question_text: For pulsar wind nebulae such as the Crab Nebula, how is the pulsar-wind magnetization σ, the ratio of Poynting flux to particle kinetic-energy flux, reduced or redistributed between the highly magnetized light-cylinder region and the wind termination shock, where efficient deceleration requires much lower magnetization, and can three-dimensional high-σ MHD evolution produce a final nebular magnetic field and non-thermal emission consistent with observations?

evidence.quote: According to theoretical models of pulsar magnetospheres, the wind is expected to be highly magnetized near the pulsar light cylinder, where clearly σ ≫ 1. On the other hand, the very first attempts at modelling the Crab nebula within the framework of ideal MHD, showed that effective deceleration of the flow at the TS is only possible if its magnetization is not too high.
However, even in the framework of 2D MHD, the estimated values of σ at the TS are still much smaller than unity, leaving the problem of efficient magnetic dissipation along the way to the shock.

In particular, it is not clear yet whether the average nebular magnetic field strength will be close to that inferred from observations (∼ 200 µG) at the final stage of the evolution, and if the synthetic non-thermal emission will match observational data in all spectral bands, thus confirming the model assumptions on the pulsar wind and emitting particles properties.

accepted.question_text: For young energetic pulsars whose magnetospheres create electron-positron pairs in cascades, what is the actual pair multiplicity κ, how does it depend on pulsar parameters, and can modeling of pulsar wind nebulae constrain κ tightly enough to determine whether any ion component of the wind can be energetically important?

evidence.quote: The exact amount of pair production in the pulsar magnetosphere and its dependence on the pulsar parameters is one of the missing ingredients in our understanding of pulsar physics and a subject of active investigation (Hibschman & Arons 2001; Timokhin & Harding 2015).

The pair production in pulsar magnetospheres is still not completely understood, but there is a general consensus that each primary electron extracted from the star surface generates a high number κ of pairs (the so called ‘pulsar pair multiplicity’) in the cascading process. For young, energetic pulsars, the expected value of the multiplicity is in the range 10^3 ≲ κ ≲ 10^7.

As a consequence they can only be at most a fraction ∼ 1/κ of the total number of the wind pairs. Nevertheless, if κ < mi/me ≈ 10^3−10^4, with mi the ion mass, the hadronic component of the wind would be energetically dominant even if numerically negligible in the wind.

accepted.question_text: In the Crab Nebula, are the low-energy particles that produce radio synchrotron emission continuously injected as part of the pulsar wind and accelerated at the termination shock, produced and reaccelerated elsewhere in the nebula such as through turbulence or thermal-filament interactions, or a relic population from an early pulsar outburst, and how can observations or three-dimensional simulations discriminate among these scenarios?

evidence.quote: Although radio emitting particles are dominant by number in the Crab nebula, their origin is still a mystery.

The question is whether radio particles are part of the pulsar outflow, and accelerated at the TS together with high-energy emitting particles, or if they are of different origin and accelerated somewhere else in the nebula.

Three different hypotheses were then considered: radio particles are injected in the nebula as part of the pulsar outflow (case A); radio particles are uniformly distributed in the nebula, produced somewhere else, for instance in the thermal filaments, and continuously accelerated by the interaction with local turbulence (case B); radio particles are a relic population, born in a primordial outburst of the pulsar during its early life, and still present thanks to their very long lifetimes against synchrotron losses (case C).
This result should be validated in the future also in three dimensions, since the stronger mixing of the magnetic field lines could in principle allow for the relic scenario to be reconsidered.

accepted.question_text: In the Crab Nebula, which acceleration mechanism or combination of mechanisms, and which locations along the wind termination shock, produce the observed broken particle spectrum, with low-energy radio-emitting particles having a flat injected slope and higher-energy particles having a steeper slope, given that driven magnetic reconnection, diffusive shock acceleration, and resonant ion-cyclotron absorption require different magnetization, striped-wind geometry, pair multiplicity, and ion-energy conditions?
accepted.context_brief: particle acceleration mechanisms at the termination shock

evidence.quote: The puzzling issue with this is the fact that relativistic magnetized shocks, as the TS is, are very hostile environments for particle acceleration, and the mechanism at the basis of the observed particle spectra is still a mystery.

The observed spectrum of the Crab nebula, similar to other PWNe, seems to suggest different acceleration mechanisms at work for low- and high-energy emitting particles, since it can be roughly modelled by assuming a broken power-law distribution function of the injected ultra-relativistic emitting particles, N(E) ∝ E^−p, with p ∼ 1.5 at low energies (for particles with E ≲ 100 GeV) and p ∼ 2.2 at higher ones (up to a few TeV).

DSA can only be effective in a few sectors of the shock, where magnetic dissipation is sufficiently strong to ensure that locally the plasma is almost unmagnetized. It is not clear however if a sufficiently large fraction of the flow satisfies this condition.
All this wealth of information will have to be incorporated in the models to obtain a reliable assessment of the particle acceleration process/es at work in the different energy ranges.

accepted.question_text: Where within the Crab Nebula are the gamma-ray flares produced, and can stochastic magnetic reconnection in thin current sheets near the termination shock or at the jet base accelerate particles to PeV energies on the observed hour-to-day timescales?

evidence.quote: Unfortunately, in spite of several attempts, no clear indication of a parent candidate location has been found yet, among the variable features observed in the optical and X-ray bands (e.g. the knots): none of these shows any special variation, during the gamma-ray flares.

The current favorite physical interpretation of the gamma-ray flares currently relies on acceleration of particles in an electric field beyond the ideal limit, since the constraint E ≤ B of relativistic MHD leads to an emission cutoff at approximately 200 MeV.

We cannot certainly determine the precise location for reconnection in the Crab nebula from this highly idealized model, but we have demonstrated that the reconnection process is able to occur on ideal time scales, independently on S_L and without invoking kinetic mechanisms, provided that during the current sheet dynamical evolution (thinning) the critical threshold of ε ∼ (S_L)^−1/3 can be reached.
Up to now the most plausible explanation seems to be violent stochastic reconnection events occurring in the TS region or at the jet base.

accepted.question_text: Can long-term three-dimensional relativistic MHD simulations of the Crab Nebula, including kink-driven magnetic-field evolution and realistic emission diagnostics, simultaneously reproduce the observed large-scale magnetic-field strength, torus and jet surface brightness, integrated synchrotron and inverse-Compton spectrum, and particle content after the nebula reaches self-similar expansion?

evidence.quote: Despite the important results introduced by this work, some problems are still unsolved. In particular, the value of the magnetic field extrapolated to the actual age of the system appears to be well below what deduced observationally (Porth, private communication). This unfortunately leaves open the question of whether the comparison of emission maps and spectra with real data will be satisfactory.
As can be seen, the synchrotron burn-off effect is clearly apparent at increasing photon energies, and emission maps are encouraging. Polar jets are well formed but the torus is quite under-luminous.
Nevertheless the volume averaged field is still lower than expected (by a factor of ∼ 2), which may indicate that the dissipation is still too high in the first stages of the evolution.

As soon as the simulation will have reached an evolved enough stage, we plan to address the issue of the integrated synchrotron and IC spectrum, and gather insight on the actual number of particles in the wind.

Extracted pair-multiplicity and radio-particle-origin candidates; kept them separate because one concerns magnetospheric pair production and the other concerns the nebular origin of radio-emitting particles.
Extracted the particle-acceleration candidate from the unresolved mechanism behind the observed broken spectrum and from the magnetization constraints on DSA and reconnection.
Extracted the gamma-ray-flare candidate from the missing parent location and the proposed but still location-uncertain reconnection explanation.
Extracted the long-term 3-D modeling validation candidate from explicit unresolved magnetic-field, emission-map, spectrum, and particle-number issues.
Expanded σ as magnetization and stated the light-cylinder-to-termination-shock dissipation problem without relying on source-internal references.
Expanded κ as pair multiplicity and included the ion-energy implication only where directly supported by the source text.
Merged the radio-origin hypotheses and the 3-D validation caveat into one self-contained question about discriminating among radio-particle origin scenarios.
Expanded the acceleration-mechanism question to include the observed broken spectrum and the physical constraints on candidate mechanisms.
Combined the flare location problem with the source-supported reconnection and ideal-tearing mechanism question.
Rewrote the 3-D modeling issue as a validation question requiring simultaneous agreement with field strength, morphology, spectrum, and particle-content observables.

Merged near-duplicate future-work statements into q_003, q_004, q_005, and q_006 while preserving separate questions for magnetization physics, pair multiplicity, radio-particle origin, acceleration mechanisms, flare origin, and 3-D model validation.
